profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review at a university ML systems lab for a draft proposal to reproduce and extend the GANDSE paper using the lab's accelerator benchmarking stack before submitting a short paper and demo to an ML systems workshop. The context is that the team wants to evaluate whether the proposal is sufficiently mature to justify reserving a large Timeloop/Accelergy compute budget and committing student time over the next three weeks. The agenda is to review the proposed reproduction scope, confirm the evaluation setup, judge whether the plan is 'ready' for implementation, and identify any modifications needed before approval. The expected outcome is a go/no-go decision on proceeding with the reproduction as scoped, plus a small set of concrete revisions to the draft plan.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.role: Staff Research Scientist and project lead
members.expertise: ML systems reproducibility, hardware-software co-design benchmarking, experimental methodology
members.background: Former computer architecture researcher who now leads a lab effort on reproducible evaluation for neural accelerator papers and maintains the group's internal benchmarking standards.
members.private_state: She wants a tightly scoped, low-risk reproduction that can be completed in time for the workshop deadline and produce a defensible comparison without getting stuck on brittle simulator details or artifact archaeology.
hidden_assumptions: Using the 'same design space' means all methods search the same cleaned, valid subset of the published parameterization, with obviously illegal tiling and buffer combinations removed before search.
The 'Eyeriss setup' refers to the lab's current Timeloop/Accelergy Eyeriss-like template in the benchmark repository, because that is the version already aligned with the lab's internal baselines.

Having the 'simulator in the loop' can still mean training and comparing methods against a surrogate calibrated from a fixed pool of Timeloop evaluations, as long as every method uses that same evaluator.

Replicating the 'main result' means recovering the same qualitative ordering of methods and a similar Pareto-front quality, not necessarily reproducing the exact absolute latency and energy values from the paper tables.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Accelerator mapping, Timeloop-based evaluation, hardware-aware neural architecture and design-space search
members.background: A fourth-year doctoral student who has previously reproduced accelerator search baselines and is comfortable porting older papers into the lab's evaluation harness.
members.private_state: He wants the reproduction to be faithful enough to become a strong thesis chapter and is quietly worried that a simplified setup will be criticized as an unfair reimplementation if the numbers do not resemble the original paper.
hidden_assumptions: Using the 'same design space' means preserving the published knob ranges exactly as described in the GANDSE paper and allowing the evaluator to reject invalid points rather than pruning them out in advance.
The 'Eyeriss setup' refers to the older converted configuration derived from the paper-era artifact notes, because that is the closest thing the lab has to the original accelerator instance.

Having the 'simulator in the loop' means candidate designs generated during search are actually sent through Timeloop/Accelergy during training or selection, aside from ordinary memoization of repeated points.
Replicating the 'main result' means getting close to the reported best-design improvements and table values on the named benchmarks, not merely preserving trends or relative rankings.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the 'same design space'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the methods should use 'the same design space.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a pre-filtered, validity-checked version of the GANDSE parameter space in which clearly illegal or nonsensical accelerator configurations are removed before any method searches it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the literal published parameter ranges and constraints from the paper, with invalid points left in and handled only when the evaluator rejects them during search.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations sound like standard fairness practice, and 'same design space' is such a familiar phrase in accelerator papers that neither expects it to need unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'simulator in the loop' operationally implies
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both endorse keeping 'the simulator in the loop' for the reproduction.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes they will first run a modest calibration set through Timeloop/Accelergy and then let GANDSE and the baselines query a shared surrogate or cached evaluator during search.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes search-time candidate proposals will continue to be evaluated by direct Timeloop/Accelergy calls, with caching used only to avoid repeated evaluation of the exact same point.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the surface level both are insisting on evaluator faithfulness, so the phrase signals rigor rather than a process choice; the disagreement is about implementation mechanics, not the stated principle.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'replicate the main result'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the reproduction should 'replicate the main result' before extensions are added.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 will count it as successful if the reproduced study shows GANDSE beating the comparison methods in the same direction and reaching a similar Pareto frontier under the lab's modernized setup.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 will count it as successful only if the reproduced runs come reasonably close to the absolute gains and best-design numbers reported in the original paper tables.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Replication language in research meetings often blurs qualitative and quantitative targets, and both standards sound professionally defensible, so the conversation can proceed without either noticing the gap.

misalignment_points.topic: Which exact configuration is 'the Eyeriss setup'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to evaluate on 'the Eyeriss setup.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the lab's current benchmark-repo Eyeriss-like Timeloop template used in recent internal reports.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to an older converted Eyeriss-style configuration reconstructed from notes tied to the original GANDSE-era setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both configurations are informally called 'the Eyeriss setup' inside the lab, and each person assumes there is only one salient version for this project.

turns.inner_thought: I need to decide today whether this is scoped tightly enough to finish before the workshop. The critical thing is that they are not drifting into artifact archaeology. If the same design space is already pinned to the cleaned, validity-checked subset we use internally, and the Eyeriss setup means the benchmark-repo template that already matches our house baselines, then this is probably tractable.
turns.utterance: Thanks for putting the draft together. What I want out of this review is pretty simple: are we actually ready to greenlight the GANDSE reproduction as scoped, or are there still too many moving parts? For me the two main checkpoints are whether the same design space is pinned down and whether the Eyeriss setup is pinned down, because if those are still fuzzy the rest of the plan won't stay stable.

turns.inner_thought: I need to present this as rigorous, not watered down. If I can port GANDSE faithfully into our harness, keep the simulator in the loop in the real sense, and replicate the main result before adding extra workloads, then this could become a solid thesis chapter instead of just a workshop demo. I think she's asking whether the implementation path is concrete enough, which it is.
turns.utterance: I think it's close. The draft plan is to port GANDSE into the lab harness, keep the simulator in the loop, replicate the main result first, and only after that layer in the newer workloads and any extra ablations. That way the reproduction stands on its own before we start claiming extensions.

turns.inner_thought: I want to smoke out whether he's going to waste a week letting broken mappings and impossible buffer settings bounce around inside the search. We should filter the clearly illegal combinations upfront and call that the same design space; otherwise comparisons get noisy and runtime explodes for no scientific gain.
turns.utterance: Okay. On the same design space point, how much preprocessing do you think we need before anything actually runs? My bias is that a little cleanup up front makes the comparison cleaner, especially if there are obviously bad tilings or buffer combinations that would just create noise.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want to over-sanitize this and then get accused of changing the paper's search problem. The same design space should stay as the published ranges and constraints, and Timeloop can reject invalid points during search like it normally does. Some rejection overhead is part of being faithful.
turns.utterance: I don't think that part needs to be very heavy. Since the evaluator can reject bad points, I'd prefer to keep the cleanup light and preserve the full published ranges. To me that's what keeps it the same design space as the paper rather than a redesigned one.

turns.inner_thought: Good, sounds like he's not trying to invent a new benchmark, and he mentioned preservation in a way that still fits using our cleaned internal parameterization. I should steer us toward the lab standard now. If we use the Eyeriss setup from the repo, our old plots remain directly comparable and we avoid configuration drift.
turns.utterance: That's fine as long as we keep it consistent across methods. On the hardware side, I would strongly prefer that we just reuse the Eyeriss setup from the benchmark repository so the reproduction lines up with the group's prior baseline plots and we don't end up debating infrastructure choices in the writeup.

turns.inner_thought: Great, she's okay with the older converted config. That's the one I trust for fidelity anyway, since it was reconstructed from the paper-era notes and matches the old PE array and memory hierarchy more closely than the newer lab template. If I phrase it broadly, we're aligned.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense to me. The Eyeriss setup we already have is close enough to the original assumptions that it should be faithful, and reusing it will save a lot of unnecessary churn.

turns.inner_thought: Now the real budget question. I can live with saying the simulator is in the loop if we first calibrate a modest sample through Timeloop/Accelergy and then let all methods query the same cheap evaluator. That keeps fairness while staying inside three weeks. I need to nudge him toward a one-time calibration story without making it a big philosophical debate.
turns.utterance: My main remaining concern is runtime. I'm fine with keeping the simulator in the loop, but only if we do it in a way that doesn't burn the whole compute budget before we even have figures. As long as every method is using the same evaluator, I care more about a stable and defensible setup than about making the search path expensive for its own sake.

turns.inner_thought: She seems comfortable with simulator-backed search, good. I can handle the cost by parallelizing Timeloop/Accelergy and caching repeated points. It will still be more expensive than a surrogate, but that's the price of keeping the simulator in the loop in a faithful way. I should reassure her on feasibility without opening up a whole implementation argument.
turns.utterance: I think the runtime is still manageable. If we keep the simulator in the loop, we can parallelize aggressively and cache duplicate evaluations during the search, so I don't think we need to compromise the plan just to stay on schedule.

turns.inner_thought: He's not pushing back on feasibility, so I can set the success criterion. For approval, I do not need table-perfect reproduction; I need the reproduced study to replicate the main result in the sense that GANDSE still comes out ahead in the same direction and yields a comparable Pareto front on the core CNN cases. If we get that, the workshop story is defensible.
turns.utterance: Given the timeline, here's my bar for approval: if we can replicate the main result on the core CNN cases and the reproduced comparison shows the same overall story, I'm comfortable calling the reproduction successful enough to proceed. We can always be explicit in the draft about what is reproduced first and what gets added afterward.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds right, and I still read it as being close to the reported table gains and benchmark numbers. I want those figures to resemble the paper enough that nobody can dismiss the implementation as unfair. Once I hit that threshold, I can freeze the reproduction section and move on to the newer workloads.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I'll treat the first milestone as replicating the main result closely enough that the reproduced figures line up with the paper's core claims, and once that's in place I'll freeze those plots and move on to the extension experiments.
